{"id":"PKIX-j32w.4","title":"Decide DANE failure mode (opportunistic vs strict-DANE vs operator-configurable)","description":"## What

When DNS resolution or DNSSEC validation fails during verify_tls_server's DANE attempt, what happens?

## Options

- **A) Opportunistic.** DNS / DNSSEC failure -> use PKIX result. Behaves like a soft suggestion. Active attacker blocking DNS can downgrade to PKIX-only. Matches RFC 7672 SMTP-DANE deployment reality. Best for adoption (won't break consumers in flaky-network environments).

- **B) Strict-DANE.** DNS / DNSSEC failure = verification failure. Refuses to fall back. Stronger security; brittle in flaky-network environments. Matches strict-security stances.

- **C) Operator-configurable, default opportunistic.** Both modes available; default opportunistic for adoption-friendliness. Strict-security deployments opt into strict mode via runtime config. Adds one knob.

## Considerations

- HTTPS-DANE has no standardized failure-mode answer.
- SMTP-DANE (RFC 7672) specifies opportunistic.
- 'Encourage DANE to spread without consumer code change' goal aligns with opportunistic default (won't break working PKIX validations).
- Strict mode is occasionally requested by regulated / high-assurance consumers.

## Deferred

Mark 2026-05-12: deferred. Needs answer before PKIX-j32w.3 (pkix-chain integration) lands.

DECIDED 2026-11-24 (Mark, interactive): Option C — operator-configurable, opportunistic default, with broken-signature handling NOT configurable.

## Reframing that produced the decision

The bead posed this as one three-way choice over 'DNS / DNSSEC failure'. Implementing DnssecStatus in pkix-dane 0.2.0 showed that 'failure' is six distinct situations, four of which are not in dispute under any of the three options. The decision surface is one row.

| Outcome | Disposition | Configurable? |
|---|---|---|
| Secure, a usable record matches | pass | no |
| Secure, usable records all mismatch | FAIL | no — this is DANE working |
| Secure, no records (authenticated denial) | use PKIX | no — domain signed 'I publish no TLSA' |
| Insecure (zone provably unsigned) | use PKIX | no — domain cannot do DANE |
| Bogus (signatures present and invalid) | FAIL | NO — see below |
| Indeterminate, or lookup failed | policy | YES — this is the decision |

## Normative spec for PKIX-j32w.3

    pub enum DaneFailurePolicy {
        Opportunistic,  // default
        Strict,
    }

- Opportunistic (Default impl): Indeterminate and lookup failure (timeout, SERVFAIL, transport error, unparsable answer) fall through to ordinary PKIX validation.
- Strict: only 'Secure, a usable record matches' passes. Indeterminate, lookup failure, Insecure and authenticated denial all fail.
- Bogus FAILS under both policies and must not be reachable by configuration.

## Why Bogus is not a policy choice

A signed zone whose signatures do not verify is an attack signal or a serious misconfiguration. If a policy could make that fall back to PKIX, an attacker able to tamper with DNS answers could switch DANE off for any domain by corrupting the response — reducing the mechanism to a suggestion for exactly the adversary it exists to stop. RFC 7671 §4.1 treats bogus as fatal. pkix-dane 0.2.0 already encodes this: DnssecStatus::permits_pkix_fallback() returns false for Bogus and true only for Insecure and Indeterminate, and the verify functions reject anything but Secure outright.

## Why opportunistic is the default, not strict

The objection to falling back is that an attacker who blocks DNS downgrades the connection to PKIX-only. That is real but bounded: the attacker still needs a CA-issued certificate for the name, so falling back leaves the caller no worse off than before DANE existed — it forgoes an upgrade rather than conceding ground. Failing instead converts any DNS flakiness into TLS failure, which breaks offline certificate audit, air-gapped validation and batch workflows that never wanted a network call.

Decisive consideration: the epic commits to a default-on dane feature with zero consumer code change. default-on combined with strict means a DNS outage breaks TLS verification for every consumer who takes a routine cargo update. default-on combined with opportunistic means a DNS outage silently yields the behavior they already had. Only the latter is a defensible default. If strict were the only mode, the feature would have to be off by default — which contradicts the epic's premise.

Strict remains available because regulated and high-assurance deployments do ask for fail-closed DANE, and they are the callers best placed to accept the brittleness.

## Consequence for the feature-gate question

This decision does not by itself settle whether the pkix-chain dane feature is default-on, but it removes the objection that made default-on dangerous. That question is tracked separately as part of PKIX-j32w.3.
